previous_argument_response.reply: The objection points to a genuine possible cost: breaking Ada’s promise to Cara may reduce overall welfare by undermining trust, causing psychic distress to Cara, and perhaps eroding social cooperation.  Under utilitarianism those indirect effects matter, but their magnitudes must be weighed against the difference in expected life-years (0.95 – 0.05 ≈ 0.9 expected life saved).  The scenario offers no numbers for the disutility of promise-breaking, so the bridge I used is the standard expected-survivors calculation together with an assumed upper bound that the welfare loss from a single broken promise is normally far smaller than the welfare gain from saving almost one additional life.  Many empirical studies on trust and well-being suggest that even large drops in reported life-satisfaction rarely equal the loss of a full life; therefore, unless promise-breaking here produces an unusually catastrophic social ripple, saving Ben remains the welfare-maximising choice.  I acknowledge the –
previous_argument_response.framework_commitment: Utilitarian principle: choose the act that maximises total expected welfare, counting all positive and negative utility (including trust and psychological effects).
previous_argument_response.reasoning_bridge: 1. Expected survivors: A0 adds 0.95 expected life; A1 adds 0.05. 2. Typical disutility from one broken promise < disutility of 0.9 expected life lost. 3. Therefore total expected welfare still higher under A0.
previous_argument_response.remaining_uncertainty: Exact utility cost of breaking Ada’s promise is unspecified; if extremely high it could overturn the comparison.
previous_argument_response.reversal_condition: If the social and psychological harm from breaking the promise is estimated to exceed the welfare of 0.9 expected life saved, preference would switch to A1.
